That was the [peace dividend](peace-dividend.qmd): the money you get from buying 1% fewer explosions. Now here is the health dividend: what happens when you spend it on medicine.

The health dividend is worth **{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_economic_value >}}**. That number is not a typo. On Wishonia, health is the default and disease is the bug report. On Earth, disease is the default and health is the dividend.

The rest of this chapter is the receipt.

## The Money: How {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}} Becomes {{< var dih_patients_fundable_annually >}} Trial Slots

This section is three division problems. On Wishonia, we teach this to children.

**Step 1.** {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}} arrives from the [peace dividend](peace-dividend.qmd).

**Step 2.** {{< var dih_treasury_medical_research_pct >}} goes to medical research after [investor and political allocations](../solution/dih.qmd), leaving {{< var dih_treasury_to_medical_research_annual >}} for trials.

**Step 3.** Subtract {{< var dfda_annual_opex >}} for [your decentralized FDA](../solution/dfda.qmd) to actually run (servers, engineers, compliance). That leaves {{< var dih_treasury_trial_subsidies_annual >}} for trial subsidies.

**Step 4.** Divide by the cost per patient. The [earlier chapters](../problem/fda-is-unsafe-and-ineffective.qmd) established that pragmatic trials cost {{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}} per patient (not the {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}} your current system charges). So:

{{< var dih_patients_fundable_annually_latex >}}

You currently enroll {{< var current_trial_slots_available >}} in clinical trials globally. With the treaty funding:

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier_latex >}}

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} more trial capacity. That is the number that changes everything downstream. Remember it.

## The Queue: {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}}, Meet {{< var dfda_queue_clearance_years >}}

You met the queue in the [untapped therapeutic frontier](../problem/untapped-therapeutic-frontier.qmd): {{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} with zero approved treatments. At your current rate of {{< var new_disease_first_treatments_per_year >}} getting their first treatment per year:

{{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years_latex >}}

![With $58.6 billion in annual R&D savings, you could run 10,000 trials and address 7,000 rare diseases. Currently you are spending that much to run far fewer trials for common diseases.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-what-var-dfda-benefit-rd-only-annual-buys-you-bw-academic.jpg)

For context, {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years_nounit >}} years ago, Shakespeare was writing plays, Galileo was building telescopes, and your species already had printing presses, universities, and intercontinental shipping. You just had not gotten around to curing most diseases. At this pace, you still will not for another {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}}.

Now apply the {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} multiplier. Instead of {{< var new_disease_first_treatments_per_year >}} diseases getting their first treatment per year, you get {{< var dfda_first_treatments_per_year >}}. The queue clears in {{< var dfda_queue_clearance_years >}} instead of {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}}.

The average untreated disease gets its first treatment {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_treatment_acceleration_years >}} earlier:

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_treatment_acceleration_years_latex >}}

Your species figured out how to split atoms in 6 years during a war, but letting a cancer patient take a pill that passed safety testing requires the gestation period of three consecutive elephants. The {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} multiplier compresses the elephant parade.

## The Efficacy Lag: {{< var efficacy_lag_years >}} of Supervised Dying

The capacity multiplier is the first component. The second: once a drug passes safety testing, your [regulatory system](../problem/fda-is-unsafe-and-ineffective.qmd) sits on it for another {{< var efficacy_lag_years >}} to confirm it works well enough, while people who could be taking it die instead.

Add the two:

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years_latex >}}

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years >}} of dying, condensed into not dying.

## The Body Count: {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved >}}

{{< var global_disease_deaths_daily >}} die from disease every day. Not all of those deaths are currently preventable, but {{< var eventually_avoidable_death_pct >}} are *eventually* avoidable with sufficient biomedical research. "Eventually avoidable" does not mean "currently preventable." It means: given enough research, these diseases have biological solutions. The only category excluded is accidents (falling off things, being hit by things). Every disease, including aging, is a biological process, and biological processes are, in principle, fixable. This is the theoretical ceiling, not a near-term promise.

Over a {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years_nounit >}}-year timeline shift, the cumulative toll:

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_latex >}}

**{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved >}}**. That is {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_dalys >}} of healthy life, and {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_suffering_hours >}} of suffering eliminated. These are cumulative, one-time benefits from permanently accelerating the discovery pipeline (the same methodology used to value smallpox eradication).

## The Price Tag on Not Being Dead

Now put a price on it. Your governments already do this when deciding whether to approve drugs, build highways, or regulate pollution. The standard rate: {{< var standard_economic_qaly_value_usd >}} per quality-adjusted life year. This is not something I invented. It is what the EPA, OECD, WHO, and NICE already use.

The world loses {{< var global_annual_daly_burden >}} DALYs per year [@ihme-gbd-2021]. {{< var eventually_avoidable_daly_pct >}} are eventually avoidable with sufficient research. At {{< var standard_economic_qaly_value_usd >}}/QALY, that is {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} per year in welfare losses. Multiply by the {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years_nounit >}}-year timeline shift:

{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_economic_value_latex >}}

Total economic value of the health dividend: **{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_economic_value >}}**.

"But that is more than global GDP!" Yes. GDP ({{< var global_gdp_2025 >}}) measures market transactions. It does not measure the value of not being dead, not being in pain, and not watching your children die of treatable diseases. The {{< var standard_economic_qaly_value_usd >}}/QALY figure is not something I invented. I just multiplied it by the number of sick people, which is also not my fault.

The only debatable input is whether the timeline shift is really ~{{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_years_nounit >}} years. See the [full derivation](../appendix/dfda-impact-paper.qmd#verification-complete-derivation-chains) for how that number is calculated, and the [Monte Carlo simulations](../appendix/dfda-impact-paper.qmd#financial-analysis-summary) for what happens when every input varies.

## The Return

![Conservative return on investment versus total return including not letting people die. One number is big, the other is astronomically big. Both beat war.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-roi-scenarios-bw-academic.jpg)

Your decentralized FDA costs {{< var dfda_annual_opex >}}/year to operate. This is roughly what your species spends annually on Halloween costumes for dogs. Less than one fighter jet. Less than what FIFA spends on "hospitality" (your word for bribing officials in a building with chandeliers). A system that could test cures for {{< var rare_diseases_count_global_nounit >}} diseases costs less to run than the outfits you put on animals that do not want to wear them.

It saves {{< var dfda_benefit_rd_only_annual >}}/year in R&D costs alone. That is **{{< var dfda_roi_rd_only >}}:1** on R&D savings, without counting a single human life. Include the lives (which you would think someone would), and the treaty's total societal benefit relative to campaign cost hits **{{< var treaty_roi_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}}:1**.

The cost per year of healthy life saved: **{{< var dfda_direct_funding_cost_per_daly >}}**. Anti-malaria bed nets, the gold standard of cost-effective interventions, cost {{< var bed_nets_cost_per_daly >}} per DALY. This system operates at {{< var treaty_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} the cost-effectiveness, at vastly greater scale. Your species gives awards to the bed net people. This costs less per life-year and nobody has heard of it.

The campaign investment: {{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}}. Even the worst case (everything goes wrong, adoption is terrible, the servers catch fire) still returns an [estimated 66:1](../appendix/dfda-impact-paper.qmd#simplified-roi-scenario). Your worst medical outcome is better than your best military one.

Every day without this system costs **{{< var dfda_rd_savings_daily >}}** in wasted trial spending alone. The regulatory lag is not a safety feature. It is a waiting room where people die. You just gave it a nicer name.

For you personally: if diseases get cured even a few years earlier, the average human gains roughly 50,000 extra hours of life. You spent 17 minutes reading this chapter. That is a 176,000x return on your time, which is more than your investment portfolio has ever achieved.

See the [full impact analysis](../appendix/dfda-impact-paper.qmd) for derivations, Monte Carlo simulations, and the comparative cost-effectiveness table.
